answer: PHP code is written inside <?php ... ?> tags. echo prints text to the screen. Save the file with a .php extension and run it in the terminal with php file.php, or open it through a web server in the browser.
keywords: how to run a php file
pitfall: PHP code will not run in an HTML file - the file name must end in .php and PHP must be installed.
title: First PHP program - echo and PHP tags

answer: Every variable starts with $. You do not declare a type - the type comes from the value. var_dump() shows both the type and the value.
code:
<?php
$name = "Prabh";   // string
$age = 19;        // int
$price = 99.5;    // float
$isStudent = true; // bool
$marks = [90, 85, 92]; // array
var_dump($name, $age, $marks);
?>
pitfall: $Name and $name are different variables - PHP variable names are case-sensitive.
title: Variables and data types

answer: In an if statement, the first block runs when the condition is true, otherwise else runs. == checks only the value, while === checks value and type - always use === where possible. For short conditions, use the ternary ?: operator.
code:
<?php
$age = 19;
if ($age >= 18) {
    echo "Adult";
} elseif ($age >= 13) {
    echo "Teen";
} else {
    echo "Child";
}
echo "\n";
// ternary
$label = ($age >= 18) ? "Adult" : "Minor";
// === vs ==
var_dump(0 == "0");   // true
var_dump(0 === "0");  // false
?>
pitfall: Writing if ($a = 5) does not compare, it assigns - write == or === for comparison.
title: if / else and comparison - == vs ===

answer: Use for when the count is known, foreach to work on every item of an array, and while to keep going until a condition stops being true. break exits the loop, continue skips one round.
code:
<?php
for ($i = 1; $i <= 3; $i++) {
    echo $i . " ";
}
$names = ["Aman", "Riya", "Prabh"];
foreach ($names as $name) {
    echo $name . "\n";
}
$count = 0;
while ($count < 3) {
    $count++;
}
?>
pitfall: Do not forget to increment the counter in a while loop, or the loop will never stop.
title: Loops - for, foreach, while

answer: A function is created with the function keyword. A parameter is the value coming in, return is the value going out. Giving a default value makes a parameter optional.
code:
<?php
function greet(string $name, string $time = "morning"): string {
    return "Good $time, $name!";
}
echo greet("Prabh");
echo greet("Prabh", "evening");
?>
pitfall: Code written after return never runs. A variable inside a function is not visible outside it.
title: Functions - create your own function

answer: To join strings in PHP, do not use +, use the dot (.). ?? means: if the left side is set and not null, use it, otherwise use the right side. % gives the remainder.
title: Operators - arithmetic, string and null coalescing

answer: Once a constant's value is set, it cannot be changed. define() works anywhere, while const is used inside classes and at the top level. A constant's name is written without $.
code:
<?php
define("SITE_NAME", "My Shop");
const TAX_RATE = 0.18;
echo SITE_NAME;
echo TAX_RATE;
?>
pitfall: Do not put $ on a constant - $SITE_NAME is wrong, SITE_NAME is correct.
title: Constants - define and const

answer: switch matches one value against many cases. match is the shorter, stricter PHP 8 version - it returns a value and compares with ===, so no break is needed.
code:
<?php
$day = "Mon";
switch ($day) {
    case "Mon": echo "Monday"; break;
    case "Sun": echo "Sunday"; break;
    default: echo "Other day";
}
$label = match ($day) {
    "Mon" => "Monday",
    "Sun" => "Sunday",
    default => "Other day",
};
echo $label;
?>
pitfall: If you forget break in switch, the next case will run too. In match, if there is no default and no case matches, an error is thrown.
title: switch and match (PHP 8)

answer: Use // or # for one line, and /* ... */ for several lines. Comments do not run; they are only for the reader.
code:
<?php
// This is a one-line comment
# This is also a one-line comment
/*
  This is a
  multi-line comment
*/
echo "Hi"; // a comment also works at the end of a line
?>
pitfall: Writing <?php inside a comment does not run the code - it stays a comment.
title: Comments - how to write notes in code

answer: Run a script in the terminal with php file.php. Words written after the command arrive in the $argv array - $argv[0] is the file's own name. To read input from the user, read fgets() from STDIN.
code:
<?php
// php greet.php Prabh
$name = $argv[1] ?? "Guest";
echo "Hello, $name!\n";
// Read input:
// echo "Enter your name: ";
// $input = trim(fgets(STDIN));
?>
pitfall: $argv is only available in the CLI, not in the browser. For browser input, use $_GET/$_POST.
title: CLI - run PHP from the terminal and $argv

answer: If the file is missing, include shows a warning and keeps going, while require stops with a fatal error. The _once version adds a file only once, so including it again does not cause a 'function already defined' error.
pitfall: Including a file with functions or classes twice without _once causes a 'cannot redeclare' error.
title: include / require - add one file to another

answer: While learning, keep error_reporting(E_ALL) and display_errors on so mistakes are visible. On a live site, keep display_errors off and write to the error log. var_dump() shows type and value, print_r() shows an array in readable form.
code:
<?php
error_reporting(E_ALL);
ini_set('display_errors', '1');
$data = ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2];
var_dump($data);
print_r($data);
// Production me:
// ini_set('display_errors', '0');
// ini_set('log_errors', '1');
?>
pitfall: Keeping display_errors on on a live site is wrong - it shows internal details to users. Only log errors there.
title: Errors and debugging - var_dump, error reporting

answer: date() gives today's date/time in a format. The DateTime class makes adding, subtracting, and comparing dates easy. For India, set the timezone to Asia/Kolkata, otherwise the server's time is shown.
code:
<?php
date_default_timezone_set("Asia/Kolkata");
echo date("d-m-Y H:i"); // 29-10-2026 10:02
$today = new DateTime();
$today->modify("+7 days");
echo $today->format("d-m-Y");
$ts = strtotime("2026-11-02");
echo date("d F Y", $ts);
?>
pitfall: Without a timezone set, date() gives the server's timezone time - in India, always set Asia/Kolkata.
title: Date and time - date(), DateTime, timezone

answer: round() rounds to the nearest value, ceil() rounds up, floor() rounds down. For security work (OTP, tokens), do not use rand(), use random_int() - it is cryptographically safe.
code:
<?php
echo round(4.6);  // 5
echo ceil(4.1);   // 5
echo floor(4.9);  // 4
echo abs(-7);     // 7
echo pow(2, 10);  // 1024
echo max(3, 9, 4); // 9
$otp = random_int(100000, 999999);
?>
pitfall: Do not use rand() for OTP/password reset tokens - it can be predicted. Use random_int().
title: Math - round, random, min/max

answer: Write (int), (float), or (string) before a value to change its type. Writing declare(strict_types=1); at the top of a file makes a wrong type passed to a function raise an error instead of being silently converted.
pitfall: (int) "abc" becomes 0 with no error - validate user input before casting it.
title: Type casting and strict types
